claims.claim: A rewrite in Go, Rust or Node would run the same libvips and the same model; I'd expect it to save a few percent per image at most
claims.about: Ruby (Sidekiq) vs Go/Rust/Node for libvips- and model-heavy image processing
claims.why: The benchmarks only measure work done inside each runtime (for example fib(20), where Ruby is 3,068 req/s and Go Gin is 18,218), not work that is mostly native libvips and model inference called from the runtime.

claims.claim: Rewriting in Go or Rust gives little speedup because the heavy work is already native
claims.about: Go/Rust vs Ruby for the processing worker
claims.why: Nothing in the measurements tests a workload where most CPU time is spent in shared native libraries, so the size of any language-level speedup can't be checked.

claims.claim: Use libvips shrink-on-load (thumbnail rather than load-then-resize); it is often a several-fold win on large photos
claims.why: libvips image operations are not benchmarked.

claims.claim: Without VIPS_CONCURRENCY=1, vips threads and Sidekiq threads oversubscribe the CPU and slow each other down
claims.why: Thread oversubscription between libvips and Sidekiq is not measured.

claims.measured: ruby-rails peak memory 175–192 MB, idle 99 MB
claims.why: The measurements give peak and idle memory over short runs, not memory growth in long-running worker processes.
Serverless platforms' cold-start behaviour is not measured; only container start-up time per server is.

claims.claim: Moving the tagging model to a Python or ONNX service is the one place a different runtime can pay off
claims.about: Python/ONNX Runtime vs Ruby for model inference
claims.why: Model inference performance is not part of the benchmarks.
